module_title: Fundamental Rights - Judicial Review, Emergency Impact, and Exceptions
introduction: This advanced level explores the definition of 'State' (Art 12), the doctrine of Judicial Review (Art 13), the impact of National Emergencies on Fundamental Rights (Arts 358 & 359), and restrictions involving Armed Forces and Martial Law (Arts 33 & 34).

core_concepts.title: Definition of State (Article 12)
core_concepts.description: Fundamental Rights are primarily guaranteed against the 'State'. Article 12 defines 'State' to include the Union and State governments, Parliaments and Legislatures, and all local or other authorities (like LIC, ONGC, SAIL).

core_concepts.title: Judicial Review (Article 13)
core_concepts.description: It declares that any law inconsistent with or in derogation of any of the Fundamental Rights shall be void. This article explicitly provides the power of 'Judicial Review' to the Supreme Court and High Courts. It includes the Doctrine of Eclipse and Doctrine of Severability.

core_concepts.title: Suspension during Emergency (Articles 358 & 359)
core_concepts.description: During a National Emergency (Art 352): Under Art 358, the freedoms under Article 19 are automatically suspended (only if emergency is declared on grounds of war/external aggression). Under Art 359, the President can suspend the right to move courts for enforcement of other Fundamental Rights.

core_concepts.title: The Immortal Articles (20 & 21)
core_concepts.description: The 44th Amendment Act (1978) established that the right to protection in respect of conviction for offenses (Art 20) and the right to life and personal liberty (Art 21) CANNOT be suspended under any circumstances, even during a National Emergency.

core_concepts.title: Armed Forces & Martial Law (Articles 33 & 34)
core_concepts.description: Article 33 empowers Parliament to restrict or abrogate the Fundamental Rights of members of armed forces, police forces, and intelligence agencies to ensure discipline. Article 34 restricts Fundamental Rights while 'Martial Law' (military rule) is in force in any area.

important_entities.name: Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973)
important_entities.significance: The Supreme Court ruled that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution (including Fundamental Rights) under Article 368, but it cannot destroy the 'Basic Structure' of the Constitution.

important_entities.name: Article 31B and the 9th Schedule
important_entities.significance: Created to protect land reform laws from judicial review. However, in the I.R. Coelho case (2007), the SC ruled that laws placed in the 9th Schedule after April 24, 1973 (Kesavananda judgment) are open to judicial review if they violate the Basic Structure.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: No, they are NOT 'absolute'; they are 'qualified'. The State can impose 'reasonable restrictions' on them based on grounds like national security, public order, decency, and morality.

The six freedoms under Article 19 are NOT suspended when a National Emergency is declared on the grounds of 'Armed Rebellion' (internal emergency). They are suspended only for 'War' or 'External Aggression'.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: These two rights always survive. No emergency can take them away.

exam_strategy_tips: In Assertion-Reasoning questions, deeply analyze the conflict between Article 13 (Judicial Review to protect FRs) and Article 368 (Parliament's amending power).
Who has the power to restrict the fundamental rights of the armed forces under Article 33? (Answer: ONLY Parliament, NOT State legislatures).
